noun:Tisch.tx: From Middle High German tisch, from Old High German tisc, from Proto-West Germanic *disk (“dish”).

adj:trans.tx: From English trans. Within German, analyzable as a shortening of transgender, transident or transgeschlechtlich.

noun:Terz.tx: Inherited from Middle High German tërzje, tërze, from Latin tertia. Doublet of Tertia. The musical sense was a later semantic loan from Italian terza.

adj:trist.tx: Borrowed from French triste. Ultimately from Latin trīstis.

noun:Turm.tx: From Middle High German turm, an East Central German variant of turn, from Old High German turn, from Old French *torn (cf. the diminutive tornele), variant of tor, from Latin turris. From the same Old French source are Dutch toren, Low German Toorn. The final -m is probably due to sporadic dissimilation; a connection with the Latin accusative turrim (as sometimes conjectured) is unlikely.

adj:tot.tx: From Middle High German tōt, from Old High German tōt, from Proto-West Germanic *daud, from Proto-Germanic *daudaz. Compare Dutch dood, Middle Low German dôt, English dead, Danish død, Norwegian Nynorsk daud.

verb:tun.tx: From Middle High German tuon, from Old High German tuon, from Proto-West Germanic *dōn, from Proto-Germanic *dōną, derived from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to put, set, place”). Cognate with English do.

adj:toll.tx: From Middle High German tol, from Old High German tol, from Proto-West Germanic *dol, from Proto-Germanic *dulaz (“dazed, foolish, crazy, stupid”).

noun:Teufel.tx: From Middle High German tiuvel, from Old High German tiufal, from Proto-West Germanic *diubul, from Latin diabolus, ultimately from Ancient Greek διάβολος (diábolos, “false accuser, slanderer”). Cognate to Bavarian Teifl, Deife, Pennsylvania German Deiwel, Dutch duivel, Old Saxon diubol (German Low German Düwel, Dîwel), English devil.

noun:Tara.tx: Borrowed from Italian tara, from Arabic طَرْح (ṭarḥ, “subtraction”).

adj:total.tx: 16th century, from Medieval Latin tōtālis, in part through Middle French total.

adv:total.tx: 16th century, from Medieval Latin tōtālis, in part through Middle French total.

noun:Tommy.tx: From English Tommy as in Tommy Atkins.

noun:Traum.tx: From Middle High German troum, Old High German troum, from Proto-West Germanic *draum, from Proto-Germanic *draumaz; akin to Low German Droom, Dutch droom, English dream, Danish drøm.

verb:trinken.tx: From Middle High German trinken, from Old High German trinkan (attested since the 8th century), from Proto-West Germanic *drinkan. Germanic cognates with identical meaning include Old Saxon drinkan (and Low German drinken), Old Dutch drinkan (and Dutch drinken, Afrikaans drink), Old English drincan (and Modern English drink), Old Frisian drinka (and West Frisian drinke), Old Norse drekka (and …

adj:trivial.tx: Borrowed from French trivial, from Latin triviālis (“common”).

adj:täglich.tx: Inherited from Middle High German tagelich, tegelich, from Old High German tagalīh. Equivalent to Tag + -lich. Cognate with English daily.

adv:täglich.tx: Inherited from Middle High German tagelich, tegelich, from Old High German tagalīh. Equivalent to Tag + -lich. Cognate with English daily.

adj:taff.tx: Borrowed from English tough. Perhaps influenced by older toff (“good, cool, well-dressed”), from Yiddish טובֿ (tof), from Hebrew טוֹב (tov, “good”). Compare Dutch tof and English toff. Doublet of zäh.

noun:Tafel.tx: From Middle High German tavel, tavele, from Old High German tavala, tabela, from Proto-West Germanic *tabulā.

verb:tappen.tx: From Middle High German tāpen with sporadic shortening before /p/ (as in Wappen, Schuppe from Middle High German wāpen, schuope). The verb is of onomatopoeic origin and comparable to the interjection tapp imitating soft walking sounds, though this is attested much later. The latter interjection is also found in Swedish tippa (“to sneak around on the toe tips”), tappa (“to tap around”), as found …

adj:traurig.tx: From Middle High German trūrec, from Old High German trūrag, from Proto-Germanic *dreuzagaz (“bloody”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰreus- (“to break, break off, crumble”). By surface analysis, Trauer + -ig. Cognate with Dutch treurig (“sad, gloomy”), Low German trurig (“sad”), Hunsrik traurich (“sad”), English dreary (“grievous, dire, appalling, drab, dark, colourless, cheerless”), Old Norse dreyrigr (“bloody”).

adv:traurig.tx: From Middle High German trūrec, from Old High German trūrag, from Proto-Germanic *dreuzagaz (“bloody”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰreus- (“to break, break off, crumble”). By surface analysis, Trauer + -ig. Cognate with Dutch treurig (“sad, gloomy”), Low German trurig (“sad”), Hunsrik traurich (“sad”), English dreary (“grievous, dire, appalling, drab, dark, colourless, cheerless”), Old Norse dreyrigr (“bloody”).

noun:Tabu.tx: Borrowed from English taboo, from Tongan tapu (“prohibited, sacred”), from Proto-Polynesian *tapu.

noun:Tag.tx: Inherited from Middle High German tac, from Old High German tag, from Proto-West Germanic *dag, from Proto-Germanic *dagaz, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *dʰegʷʰ-. In earlier legal documents since Middle High German, Tag was frequently used in the meaning of “a fixed day for meeting, debate, or appointment,” which was associated with words like Reichstag, Landtag, later Ratstag, and tagen …

intj:Tag.tx: Abbreviation of the greeting guten Tag (“good day”).

noun:Tal.tx: Inherited from Middle High German tal, from Old High German tal. Cognate with Danish dal, Dutch dal, English dale, Swedish dal.

noun:Taler.tx: Clipping of Joachimstaler, the name of a coin first minted in Joachimsthal, Bohemia around 1518, soon after the discovery of silver deposits there. Ultimately from Joachim + Thal (“valley”), now spelled Tal. Cognate to Low German Daler. Doublet of Dollar

noun:Tang.tx: Of North Germanic origin, such as Danish tang or Swedish tång, from Old Norse þongull, þang, from Proto-Germanic *þanga, from Proto-Indo-European *tenk- (“to thicken, be solid”), related to Proto-Germanic *þinhaną.

noun:Tapir.tx: Borrowed from French tapir, from Old Tupi tapi'ira.

noun:Tasche.tx: From Middle High German tasche, from Old High German taska, tasca. Further origin unknown. Perhaps from Proto-Germanic *taskǭ. Cognate with Dutch tas, Hunsrik Tasch, Middle Low German tasche (“bag, pouch”), Old Norse taska (“bag, purse”) (probably borrowed from Low German). Compare English tasse (“plate armor, which protects the thighs”).

noun:Tasse.tx: From Late Middle High German *tasse, which is not attested as a simplex before the 16th c., but required by the diminutive tesschichyn (mid-15th c.). Further from Middle French tasse (14th c.), from Arabic طَاس (ṭās), variant of طَسْت (ṭast), from Middle Persian tšt' (tašt). Cognate with Modern French tasse, Dutch tas, dialectal English tass. Distantly related with Docht, Technologie, Text.

noun:Taste.tx: From Italian tasto (“key”), from the verb tastare, from Vulgar Latin *tastāre (“to touch, feel”), from *taxitāre, from Latin taxāre (“to touch sharply”), from tangere (“to touch”). Related with older German tasten, which is from the same Latin verb through Old French.

noun:Tat.tx: From Middle High German tāt, from Old High German tāt (akin to Old Saxon dād), from Proto-West Germanic *dādi. Compare Low German Daad/Daat, Dutch daad, English deed, Danish dåd, Gothic *𐌳𐌴𐌸𐍃 (*dēþs), and Ancient Greek θέσις (thésis, “arrangement”).

noun:Tau.tx: From Middle High German tou, from Old High German tou, from Proto-Germanic *dawwaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewh₂- (“smoke, haze”). Compare Low German Dau, Dutch dauw, English dew, compare also Danish dug.

noun:Team.tx: Ca. 1900, from English team. Doublet of Zaum.

noun:Tee.tx: Ultimately from Hokkien 茶 (tê), probably through Dutch thee. Attested since the 17th century.

noun:Teller.tx: From Middle High German teller (“plate”), from Middle French tailloir (“plate, cutting board”).

noun:Tenno.tx: Borrowed from Japanese 天皇(てんのう) (tennō), from Middle Chinese 天皇 (then hwang) with the original sense of “heavenly sovereign”.

noun:Tenor.tx: From Middle High German tenōr, from Italian tenore, from Latin tenor.

noun:Termite.tx: From the Late Latin termes, late variant of the Classical Latin tarmes (“woodworm”).

noun:Test.tx: Borrowed from English test, from Old French test (“pot; melting pot, especially one in which metals were tried”), from Latin testum (“pot”). Compare etymology 2 below. The development from “melting pot” to “procedure of testing metals” also happened natively in earlier German, but the further generalisation is exclusively English.

noun:Text.tx: From Middle High German text, from Latin textus.

noun:Theater.tx: Borrowed from French théâtre, utimately from Ancient Greek θέατρον (théatron, “a place for viewing”), from θεάομαι (theáomai, “to see, watch, observe”).

noun:Theorem.tx: Borrowed from Late Latin theōrēma, from Ancient Greek θεώρημα (theṓrēma, “speculation, proposition to be proved”) (Euclid).

noun:Thesaurus.tx: 16th century, borrowed from Latin thesaurus. Doublet of Tresor and Tresen.

noun:Thing.tx: 18th century, learned borrowing from Old High German thing and Old Norse þing, both from Proto-Germanic *þingą. Doublet of inherited Ding.

noun:Thorn.tx: From English thorn from Middle English thorn, þorn, from Old English þorn, þyrn (“thorn”), from Proto-Germanic *þurnuz, from Proto-Indo-European *tr̥nós, from *(s)ter- (“stiff”).

noun:Tide.tx: Borrowed from German Low German Tide, a variant of Getide, from Middle Low German getīde, equivalent to modern German ge- + Zeit (“time”). Cognate with Dutch tij, getijde, and English tide.

noun:Tier.tx: From Middle High German tier, from Old High German tior, from Proto-West Germanic *deuʀ, from Proto-Germanic *deuzą, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewsóm. Cognate to English deer.

noun:Tilde.tx: 19th century, from Spanish tilde, from Latin titulus. Doublet of Titel (“title”) and Tüttel (“dot”).

noun:Titan.tx: Borrowed from Latin Tītān, Tītānus, from Ancient Greek Τιτάν (Titán).

noun:Tod.tx: From Middle High German tōt, from Old High German tōd, from Proto-West Germanic *dauþu, from Proto-Germanic *dauþuz. Compare Old Saxon dōth, Dutch dood, English death, Danish død.

noun:Tomahawk.tx: Borrowed from English tomahawk, that from an Eastern Algonquian word.

noun:Tomate.tx: Borrowed from French tomate or Spanish tomate, from Classical Nahuatl tomatl (“tomatillo”), the tomato proper being xītomatl.

noun:Ton.tx: With irregular t- (as in tausend) and widespread dialectal -ā- → -ō- from Middle High German dāhen, tāhen, inflected form of dāhe, tāhe, from Old High German thāha, dāha, tāha, from Proto-Germanic *þanhǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *tenk- (“to thicken, be solid”), related to *þinhtaz (“dense, tight”). Cognate with Old English þō, Old Norse þá, Gothic 𐌸𐌰𐌷𐍉 (þāhō). The oldest spelling is Toh(e)n, …

noun:Tonne.tx: From Middle High German tunne, from Old High German tunna, from Latin tunna. A chiefly northern (i.e. Central German) word, later reinforced by Middle Low German tunne, tonne and, in the sense “metric ton”, by French tonne.

noun:Tor.tx: From Middle High German and Old High German tor, from Proto-West Germanic *dor, from Proto-Germanic *durą.

noun:Tornado.tx: Borrowed from Spanish tornado in the 19th century, from English tornado, from Spanish tronada.

noun:Torpedo.tx: Borrowed from English torpedo, from Latin.

noun:Torte.tx: 15th century, from Middle French tarte, tourte, later reinforced by Italian torta, all from Late Latin torta (“cake, round loaf”).

noun:Tour.tx: 16th century, borrowed from Middle French tour. Feminine gender after words such as Reise, Fahrt, Drehung.

noun:Tram.tx: Borrowed from English tram, related to Tram m (“beam”) (etymology 2).

noun:Transfer.tx: 18th century, common since early 20th century. Borrowed from English transfer, from Latin transferre. The verb transferieren is older and directly from Latin.

noun:Transformation.tx: From Latin trānsfōrmātiō. Compare Hunsrik Transformazion.

noun:Transit.tx: Borrowed from Italian transito, from Latin trānsitus.

noun:Translation.tx: Borrowed from French translation, from Latin trānslātiō.

noun:Transport.tx: Borrowed from French transport, influenced by Italian traspòrto. First attested in the 17th century.

noun:Trauma.tx: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek τραῦμα (traûma, “wound”).

noun:Trend.tx: Unadapted borrowing from English trend, ca. 1925.

noun:Triumph.tx: 15th century, from Latin triumphus. Doublet of Trumpf.

noun:Troll.tx: 18th century, from Danish trold, Swedish troll, both from Old Norse trǫll, from Proto-Germanic *truzlą. Influenced by a native word for “coarse, boorish person”, attested in Upper German dialects from the 15th century, which is probably cognate to the former. The internet sense after English troll, from the Old Norse.

noun:Trottoir.tx: Borrowed from French trottoir. Compare dialectal Trottwa.

noun:Trunk.tx: From Middle High German trunc, from Old High German trunk, from the root of trinken (“to drink”). Doublet of Drink.

noun:Tsunami.tx: Borrowed from Japanese 津波 (tsunami, “seismic sea wave”, literally “harbour wave”).

noun:Tuba.tx: 18th century, learned borrowing from Latin tuba.

noun:Turban.tx: 16th century as Turbant etc. from Italian turbante, from Ottoman Turkish دلبند (dülbend), from Persian دلبند (dolband). The contemporary form (late 17th c.) follows French turban.

noun:Twist.tx: Borrowed from English twist. Doublet of Zwist.

noun:Type.tx: Borrowed from French type, from Latin typus, from Ancient Greek τῠ́πος (tŭ́pos).

adj:trocken.tx: From Middle High German trucken, trocken, from Old High German truckan, trokkan (“dried out, parched, thirsty, dry”), from Proto-West Germanic *drukn, from Proto-Germanic *druknaz, *druhnaz (“dry”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰerǵʰ- (“to strengthen; become hard or solid”), from *dʰer- (“to hold, hold fast, support”). The form trucken was originally predominant, but the word eventually became …

noun:Taliban.tx: From Pashto طالبان (tālibān), plural of طالب (tālib, “disciple”).

noun:Techtelmechtel.tx: From Austrian Dechtlmechtl. The word probably derives from Yiddish פֿאַרדעכטיק (fardekhtik, “hidden, secret”), from דאַך (dakh, “roof, covering”).

noun:Türke.tx: Ultimately from Old Anatolian Turkish ترك (türk), although the intermediate steps are unclear. Possibly borrowed directly into Middle High German during the Crusades.

noun:Typ.tx: Borrowed from Latin typus (“figure, pattern”), from Ancient Greek τύπος (túpos, “type; impression”). Compare French type (“guy, bloke”), and Spanish tipo.

noun:Tür.tx: From Middle High German tür, from Old High German turi, from Proto-West Germanic *dur. Compare English door.

noun:Topf.tx: From Middle High German topf, from Old High German *topf, from Proto-West Germanic *dopp, from Proto-Germanic *duppaz (“hollow, bowl”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewb- (“deep, hollow”). Cognate with Dutch dop (“little cup, thimble”), Low German Dopp (“shell, pod, bowl”), Saterland Frisian Dop (“shell, pod, bowl”), English dop (“cup in which a diamond is cut”). Both in historic sources and modern …

verb:tauschen.tx: From Middle High German tūschen, related to täuschen (“to deceive”) (from tiuschen).

noun:Taktik.tx: 18th century, from French tactique, from Ancient Greek τακτική (τέχνη) (taktikḗ (tékhnē)).

noun:Teewurst.tx: From Tee (“tea”) + Wurst (“sausage”). Probably from the habit of serving sandwiches at teatime.

noun:Tausend.tx: Nominalization of tausend. The interjection is short either for potz tausend Teufel (16th century) or for Middle High German tūsentlisteler, later Tausendkünstler (“the devil as a master of a thousand ruses, arts”).

num:tausend.tx: From Middle High German tūsunt, from Old High German dūsunt, from Proto-West Germanic *þūsundi, from Proto-Germanic *þūsundī. Compare Old Saxon thūsund, Dutch duizend, West Frisian tûzen, English thousand, Danish tusind.

noun:Tastatur.tx: From older Italian tastatura; compare tastiera. Analysable as Taste (“key, button”) + -tur.

verb:tasten.tx: From northern Middle High German and Middle Low German tasten, from Middle Dutch tasten, from Old French taster, from Vulgar Latin *tastare, from *taxitare, from Latin taxare. Cognate with Dutch tasten, French tâter, English taste.

noun:Taube.tx: From Middle High German tūbe, from Old High German tūba, from Proto-West Germanic *dūbā. Cognate with German Low German Duuv, Dutch duif, English dove, Danish due, Norwegian Bokmål due, Norwegian Nynorsk due, Swedish duva, Alemannic German Tuub, Yiddish טויב (toyb).

noun:Turteltaube.tx: From Middle High German turteltūbe, türteltūbe, from Old High German turtiltūba, turtultūba, from Proto-West Germanic *turtiladūbā (“turtle dove”).

noun:Tanz.tx: From Middle High German tanz, from Middle Dutch dans, from Old French danse, dancier, equivalent to a deverbal from tanzen. See tanzen for more.

verb:tanzen.tx: From Middle High German tanzen, from Old French dancer; the adapted onset t- in Upper German dialects (and standard German) proves that the word was not borrowed directly from the French word, but via Middle Low German or Middle Dutch dansen and Central German.

verb:tapezieren.tx: From obsolete tapissieren, borrowed in the 16th century from Middle French tapisser, a derivative of Old French tapiz, from Ancient Greek ταπήτιον (tapḗtion). The modern German form was influenced by the somewhat older noun Tapete and possibly Italian tappezzare.

noun:Tapete.tx: 15th century. From Latin tapēte (“wall hanging cloth”), from tapēs (“carpet”), from Ancient Greek τάπης (tápēs, “carpet, rug”).

noun:Trichter.tx: From Middle High German trihter, from Old High German trahtāri, trahteri, thretāri, trehteri, trihteri, from Proto-West Germanic *trahtārī (“funnel”). Cognate with English trajectory.

verb:tauchen.tx: From Middle High German tūchen, touchen, from Old High German *tūhhan – only in firtūhhan (“to sink into oblivion”), intūhhan (“to immerse”) –, from Proto-West Germanic *dūkan. Cognate to Dutch duiken, Swedish dyka. The word had become obsolete in Upper German, but was later reintroduced on the basis of Central German dūchen, tūchen and Middle Low German dūken, which had remained common. In the …

noun:Tarnkappe.tx: From Middle High German tarnkappe. The first element is likely related to Proto-West Germanic *darnī (“secret, hidden”) and the second element is from Kappe. By surface analysis, tarnen + Kappe.

verb:tarnen.tx: Early 20th century, a borrowing (inspired by older Tarnkappe) from Middle High German tarnen, from Old High German *tarnōn, from Proto-West Germanic *darnōn. Cognate with English darn.

noun:Tanne.tx: From Middle High German tanne, from Old High German tanna, from Proto-West Germanic *dannā, from Proto-Germanic *dannǭ, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *(s)dʰonu (“fir”). Per this hypothesis, related to Hittite 𒄑𒋫𒈾𒀀𒌑 (^(GIŠ)ta-na-a-ú /⁠tanau⁠/, “fir”), Breton tann (“sessile oak”), Avestan 𐬚𐬀𐬥𐬎𐬎𐬀𐬭𐬆 (θanuuar^ə, “bow”), Sanskrit धनु (dhánu), perhaps Latin femur (“thigh”).

noun:Tinte.tx: From Middle High German tincte, tinte, dinte, etc., from Old High German tincta, borrowed from Medieval Latin tincta, from tingō (“to wet, dip, dye, tinge”).

noun:Tintenfisch.tx: Compound of Tinte (“ink”) + -n- + Fisch (“fish”). Attested from the 17th century, as dinten Fisch, equated with Meerspin "sea-spider" in Joseph du Chesne or Duchesne (Josephus Quercetanus), Johan Adolff Ringelstein Diaeteticon polyhistoricum (Straßburg, 1625), p. 218. Glossed as synonymous with sepia (cuttlefish) or Sepia in Tilesius, Verzeichnis verschiedener Fische und Krebse des adriatischen …

noun:Trommel.tx: From late Middle High German trummel, diminutive of Old High German trumme, probably of imitative origin. Compare trommeln.

verb:töten.tx: From Middle High German tœten, tœden, from Old High German *tōten, tōden, from Proto-West Germanic *daudijan ~ *dauþijan. By surface analysis, tot (“dead”) + -en. Cognate with Dutch doden, Old Norse deyða, Gothic 𐌳𐌰𐌿𐌸𐌾𐌰𐌽 (dauþjan). Compare also English deaden.

noun:Trauer.tx: From Middle High German trūre (“mourning”), from Old High German trūrēn (“to mourn”), from Proto-West Germanic *drūrēn (“to fall”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *dʰrews- (“to break apart”).

noun:Tropfen.tx: From Middle High German tropfen, tropfe, from Old High German tropfo, from Proto-West Germanic *dropō, from Proto-Germanic *drupô. Akin to English drop.

noun:Treibsand.tx: From Middle High German tripsant, trybsand (both Central German, 14th c.). Like all High German attestations before the 16th century, these seem to be equivalent to modern Trieb + Sand, which is notable because Middle High German trip was commonly used of the driving of livestock only. Hence, possibly from Middle Low German drifsant (15th c., could be drīfsant), dryffsandt (16th c.), from …

noun:Töpfer.tx: From Early New High German töpfer, topfer, from Middle High German toppfer, topper. Equivalent to Topf + -er.

adv:tags.tx: From Middle High German tages, from Old High German dages. Equivalent to Tag + -s.

noun:Torschlusspanik.tx: From Tor + Schluss + Panik, literally “gate-shut panic”. For safety reasons city gates used to be shut at nightfall (Torschluss, from Tor + Schluss), leaving latecomers no other choice than to stay outside, thereby exposing them to various dangers.

verb:triefen.tx: From Middle High German triefen, from Old High German triufan, triofan, from Proto-West Germanic *dreupan. Akin to Old Saxon driopan and Dutch druipen.

verb:treiben.tx: From Middle High German trīben, from Old High German trīban, from Proto-West Germanic *drīban. Cognates Cognate with Low German drieven, Dutch drijven, English drive, Danish drive, Swedish driva. More at drive.

verb:tauen.tx: From late Middle High German touwen (“to thaw, dew”), a merger of two verbs: * touwen (“to dew”), from Old High German touwōn, from Proto-West Germanic *dauwēn, from Proto-Germanic *dawwāną. * douwen (“to thaw”), from Old High German douwen, from Proto-West Germanic *þauwjan, from Proto-Germanic *þawjaną. The merger started in Central German dialects, many of which had d- in both verbs. The …

verb:taufen.tx: From Middle High German and Old High German toufen, from Proto-West Germanic *daupijan. Compare Old Saxon dōpian, Dutch dopen, Old English dīepan, Gothic 𐌳𐌰𐌿𐍀𐌾𐌰𐌽 (daupjan).

verb:taugen.tx: From Middle High German tougen, tugen, tügen, from Old High German tugan (attested since the 9th century); from Proto-Germanic *duganą, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewgʰ- (“to produce”). Germanic cognates include Yiddish טויגן (toygn), Old Saxon dugan, Dutch deugen (> Afrikaans deug), Old English dugan (obsolete Modern English dow), Old Norse duga (> Icelandic duga, Faroese duga, Norwegian duge, …

verb:teilen.tx: From Middle High German and Old High German teilen, from Proto-West Germanic *dailijan (“to divide, part, deal”). Cognate with English deal.

verb:tragen.tx: From Middle High German tragen, from Old High German tragan, from Proto-West Germanic *dragan, from Proto-Germanic *draganą (“to draw, drag”). Cognates Related to Bavarian trågn, Dutch dragen, English draw, drag, Danish drage, Icelandic draga.

verb:träumen.tx: From Middle High German and Old High German troumen, from Proto-West Germanic *draumijan. Akin to Dutch dromen, English dream, and Swedish drömma.

noun:Teil.tx: From Middle High German teil, from Old High German teil, from Proto-West Germanic *daili, akin to Old Saxon dēl, cognate with English deal, Dutch deel, Low German Deil, Swedish del, Norwegian Bokmål del, Norwegian Nynorsk del, Danish del. Doublet of Deal.

noun:Traube.tx: From Middle High German trūbe, from Old High German drūbo, thrūbo, from Proto-West Germanic *þrūbō.

noun:Tochter.tx: Inherited from Old High German tohter. Compare Dutch dochter, English daughter, Swedish dotter. * (subsidiary): ellipsis of Tochtergesellschaft

adj:tief.tx: From Middle High German tief, tiuf, going back to Old High German tiuf, tiof, inherited through Proto-West Germanic *deup and ultimately deriving from Proto-Germanic *deupaz, from Pre-Germanic *dʰewbʰnós, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewbʰ-. Compare Dutch diep, Low German diep, deep, English deep, Danish dyb, Norwegian dyp, Icelandic djúpur.

adj:taub.tx: From Middle High German toup, toub, from Old High German toub, from Proto-West Germanic *daub, from Proto-Germanic *daubaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewbʰ- (“to whisk, be obscured”); cognate to English deaf, Swedish döv. Doublet of doof.

adj:teuer.tx: From Middle High German tiure, from Old High German tiuri, from Proto-West Germanic *diurī, from Proto-Germanic *diurijaz, akin to Old Saxon diuri, compare Dutch duur, English dear, Icelandic dýr, and Swedish dyr.

noun:Tuch.tx: From Middle High German tuoch, from Old High German tuoh, from Proto-West Germanic *dōk (“cloth”). Compare Dutch doek (“cloth, canvas”), English duck. More at duck, dook.

noun:Thron.tx: From Middle High German thrōn, trōn, from Old French tron, from Latin thronus, from Ancient Greek θρόνος (thrónos, “seat, place of honour”).

verb:treten.tx: From Middle High German trëten, from Old High German trëtan, from Proto-West Germanic *tredan, from Proto-Germanic *trudaną. Cognate with English tread.

prep:trotz.tx: Ellipsis of zum Trotz (dem) or from constructions with the dative verb trotzen. Compare trotzdem.

adj:tapfer.tx: From Middle High German tapfer, from Old High German tapfar, from Proto-Germanic *dapraz.

noun:Tadel.tx: Inherited from Middle High German tadel, a borrowing from Middle Low German which replaced Middle High German zadel, from Old High German zādal; further etymology unknown.

noun:Tabak.tx: 16th century, from Spanish tabaco, in part through French tabac.

noun:Talg.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German talch, from Old Saxon *talg, from Proto-West Germanic *talg, from Proto-Germanic *talgaz. More at tallow.

noun:Tatze.tx: From Middle High German tatze, of uncertain origin. Perhaps related to tappen (“to pad, walk softly”). Or, a children's slang/imitative word (lautmalend).

noun:Taufe.tx: From Middle High German toufe, from Old High German toufī, from Proto-West Germanic *daupīni (“dipping, immersion”). Upper German form with lack of umlaut before a labial; reinforced probably by the fact that the Central German variants clashed with Teufe, older form of Tiefe (“depth”).

noun:Teer.tx: Borrowed from Low German and Middle Low German ter, from Old Saxon *tero, from Proto-West Germanic *teru, from Proto-Germanic *terwą.

noun:Teich.tx: From Middle High German tīch, from Old High German tīh, from Proto-West Germanic *dīk, from Proto-Germanic *dīkaz. Doublet of Deich, which is the same word from a West Central German source. Cognate with Yiddish טײַך (taykh), Dutch dijk, English ditch, English dyke, dike.

noun:Teig.tx: From Middle High German teic, from Old High German teig, teic (attested since the 9th century); from Proto-Germanic *daigaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeyǵʰ- (“to knead, to mold, to form”). Cognate with English dough, Dutch deeg, Old English dāg, Old Norse deig (whence Icelandic deig, Faroese deiggj, Norwegian deig, Swedish deg, Danish dej), Gothic 𐌳𐌰𐌹𐌲𐍃 (daigs). Also compare Finnish taikina and …

noun:Teppich.tx: From Middle High German teppich, tepich, teppech, tepech, tepch, teppch; from Old High German teppih, tepich, teppech; from Medieval Latin tapicus; from Latin tapes.

noun:Torf.tx: From Middle Low German torf, from Old Saxon turf, *torf, from Proto-West Germanic *turb, from Proto-Germanic *turbz, from Proto-Indo-European *derbʰ-. The Proto-Germanic etymon was possibly inherited in Old High German as zurf (one attestation). More at turf.

noun:Tracht.tx: From Middle High German traht(e), from Old High German trahta, from Proto-Germanic *drahtuz, from the verb *draganą, whence modern tragen, thus originally “that which is borne/worn/carried”. Cognate with Dutch dracht, English draught. Not related to German trachten (“to seek, strive”), although certain descendants (Eintracht, Niedertracht, Zwietracht) are associated with that verb by contemporary speakers.

noun:Träne.tx: From Middle High German træne (“tears”), plural of trān m, a Central German variant of trahen, from Old High German trahan (“tear”), from Proto-West Germanic *trahnu (“tear”). Doublet of Tran (“fish oil”, from Low German). Cognate with Dutch traan (“tear; fish oil”), Hunsrik Dreen. Possibly also related with German Zähre, English tear.

noun:Treppe.tx: Attested since the 12th century, from Middle High German treppe, trappe, from Old High German trappa, from Proto-West Germanic *trappā.

noun:Trieb.tx: From Middle High German trīp, from trīben, related to treiben.

noun:Trog.tx: From Middle High German troc, from Old High German trog, from Proto-West Germanic *trog, from Proto-Germanic *trugaz. Akin to Dutch trog, English trough, Danish trug, Swedish tråg.

noun:Trost.tx: From Middle High German trōst, from Old High German trōst, from Proto-West Germanic *traust, from Proto-Germanic *traustą.

noun:Truhe.tx: From Middle High German truhe, from Old High German truha, with Verner alternation from the root of Trog (“trough”). The Old High German word may have been influenced semantically by the (originally unrelated) descendant of Proto-Germanic *þrūhs, whence Old English þrūh and dialectal English through (“coffin”). Chiefly restricted to Upper German dialects, Truhe spread northwards only during the …

noun:Trümmer.tx: Plural of Trumm (Middle High German drum, Old High German trum, Proto-Germanic *þrum-), which has acquired a separate meaning. The Middle High German plural was drum or drumer, Early New High German trumer, trumeren, trummer, trimmer, trümmern. The new singular Trümmer (either feminine, masculine or neuter) arises in the 18th century (Klopstock). The singular remained in common use until the end …

noun:Trumpf.tx: From a popular pronunciation of Triumph, from Latin triumphus. The sense developed under the influence of Middle French triumphe.

noun:Truthahn.tx: From trut + Hahn (“rooster”). The first element is either imitative of the turkey’s call to its young (cf. the etymology of Pute) or alternatively from Middle Low German drōten (“threaten”), improperly adapted to High German, in reference to the male turkey’s seemingly aggressive behavior.

noun:Tulpe.tx: Borrowed from Dutch tulp, from Ottoman Turkish دلبند (dülbend), from Persian دلبند (dolband). Doublet of Tulipan.

noun:Tugend.tx: From Middle High German tugent, from Old High German tugund (“virtue, power”), from Proto-Germanic *dugunþō (“usefulness, virtue”). Cognate with English douth, dought.

noun:Tümpel.tx: From Middle High German tümpfel, from Old High German tumphilo, from Proto-West Germanic *dumpil, from Proto-Germanic *dumpilaz, related to *deupaz (“deep”). The regular Upper German form is Tümpfel, which is now obsolete in standard usage; the unshifted -p- is from Central German dialects. Cognate with English dimple.

noun:Tüte.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German tûte, tǖte (“horn, conical paper bag”). Cognate with English tote (“bag”), Dutch tuit (“spout”). Further origin unknown, though has been suggested to be part of a sound-symbolic family of words including Zitze (“teat”).

noun:Tiefe.tx: From Middle High German tiefe, alteration (based on the form of the adjective) of tiufe, from Old High German tiufī. Analysable as tief (“deep”) + -e (“-ness”).

noun:Treue.tx: From Middle High German triuwe, from Old High German triuwa, from Proto-West Germanic *treuwu, from Proto-Germanic *trewwō.

verb:toben.tx: From Middle High German toben, from Old High German tobēn, tobōn from Proto-West Germanic *dobēn. Cognate with Middle Low German dōven, Alemannic German tobe.

verb:treffen.tx: From Middle High German trëffen, from Old High German trëffan, from Proto-West Germanic *drepan, from Proto-Germanic *drepaną, whence also English drub.

verb:trauen.tx: From Middle High German trūwen, from Old High German trūwēn, from Proto-West Germanic *trūwēn, from Proto-Germanic *trūwāną.

verb:trennen.tx: From Middle High German trennen, from Old High German trennen, from Proto-West Germanic *trannijan, from Proto-Germanic *trannijaną. Cognate with German Low German trennen, Dutch tornen (archaic tarnen, from Middle Dutch ternen, metathesis of older trennen).

verb:tropfen.tx: From Middle High German tropfen, from Old High German tropfōn. Synchronically analyzable as a verbal of Tropfen (“drop”).

verb:trösten.tx: From Middle High German trœsten, from Old High German trōsten, from Proto-West Germanic *traustijan, from Proto-Germanic *traustijaną. By surface analysis, Trost + -en.

noun:Trotz.tx: From Middle High German traz, from an unknown source whence also Dutch tarten (“to provoke, dare”). Pokorny connects the words to Proto-Indo-European *der- (“to tear”) and compares them with Old English teart (“tart”), while Pfeifer suspects an onomatopoeic origin (DWDS). Others have compared Proto-Germanic *þrawaz (“stubborn, obstinate”).

adj:trüb.tx: From Middle High German trüebe, from Old High German truobi, from Proto-West Germanic *drōbī. Cognate with Dutch droef (“sad, miserable”), English droff (“turbid, sorrowful, sad”).

verb:trügen.tx: From Middle High German triegen, from Old High German triugan, triogan, from Proto-West Germanic *dreugan. The expected form is earlier modern German triegen, the vocalism -ü- being due to influence by lügen (“to lie, to tell lies”), itself originally liegen and thus a rhyming word.

noun:Tagundnachtgleiche.tx: From Tag (“day”) + und (“and”) + Nacht (“night”) + Gleiche (“equality, sameness”).

noun:Teddybär.tx: Partial calque of English teddy bear; from Bär.

verb:tapen.tx: From Tape + -en, after English to tape.

verb:testen.tx: By surface analysis, Test + -en. Diachronically, from English test + -en.

verb:tosen.tx: From Middle High German, from Old High German, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *þausōną (“to surge, roar, flow”), which is imitative. See also Old English þys (“tempest, storm”), Old Norse þyssa (“uproar, tumult”), Icelandic þysja (“to rush”).

verb:traben.tx: From Middle High German traben, draben, from Old High German *drabōn (“to press; stamp; stomp”), from Proto-Germanic *þrabōną (“to press, drive, compel”). Cognate with Old English þrafian (“to urge, compel; argue”). More at thrave.

verb:turnen.tx: From Middle High German *turnen, from Old High German turnēn, borrowed from Latin tornō (“to turn, lathe”). Cognate with English turn. Semantically, compare English tumble.

noun:Tube.tx: Later 19th century, borrowed from English tube. Doublet of Tubus. The pronunciation follows the underlying Latin tubus, tuba; compare etymology 2 below.

intj:tja.tx: Probably from an onomatopoeia for clicking one’s tongue, which is used with the same meaning. Perhaps also a variant of ja (“yes”). Similar expressions are found in nearby Germanic languages and in Finnish, suggesting an areal feature.

verb:trimmen.tx: Late 19th century, at first in nautical parlance, from English trim, from Middle English trimmen, from Old English trymman. For the sense “work out” compare the Dutch entry above.

noun:Transvestit.tx: Coined in 1910 by German sexologist Magnus Hirschfeld. Influenced by 18th-century French word travesti.

noun:Trigonometrie.tx: From 1610s, from New Latin trigōnometria, from Ancient Greek τρίγωνον (trígōnon, “triangle”) + μέτρον (métron, “measure”).

noun:Tunichtgut.tx: Univerbation of tu nicht gut, literally “don't do well”.

noun:Tamarinde.tx: From Medieval Latin tamarindus, possibly via Italian tamarindo.

noun:Tukan.tx: Borrowed from Spanish tucán, from Paraguayan Guarani tukã.

noun:Thymian.tx: From Middle High German thimiān, alteration of thymiāme, from Latin thymiama, from Ancient Greek θυμίαμα (thumíama, “incense”). The sense through association with thymum, θύμον (thúmon, “thyme”), probably already in Latin (if not Greek itself), as thyme was a commonly used incense. Whether the two words are originally related is uncertain.

adj:traditionell.tx: By surface analysis, Tradition + -ell. Borrowed from French traditionnel.

noun:Taifun.tx: Borrowed from English typhoon; see there for further etymology.

noun:Toleranz.tx: From Latin tolerantia. By surface analysis, tolerant + -anz or tolerieren + -anz

noun:Tresor.tx: 19th century, borrowed from French trésor, which see. Doublet of Tresen and Thesaurus.

verb:täuschen.tx: From Middle High German tiuschen, from a Middle Low German dialect, cognate with tauschen (“to trade”), with both terms of unknown further origin.

noun:Trampolin.tx: 19th century, from Italian trampolino. Related to German trampeln.

verb:trampeln.tx: From Middle High German trampeln. Equivalent to trampen + -eln (frequentative suffix). The unshifted -mp- is regular in Central and Low German, but is invariably found in Upper German dialects, too. The onomatopoetic character of the verb does not sufficiently explain this, particularly as Upper German has a shifted ablaut variant trumpfen (“to trample”). Perhaps trampen, trampeln were originally …

noun:Taschentuch.tx: Tasche (“pocket”) + Tuch (“cloth”). Compare Dutch zakdoek in the same vein.

noun:Tiergarten.tx: From Tier (“animal”) + Garten (“garden”). Cognate with Dutch diergaarde (“zoo”).

noun:Tempel.tx: From Middle High German tempel, from Old High German tempal, from Proto-West Germanic *templ (“temple”).

verb:transformieren.tx: From Middle High German [Term?], from Latin trānsformāre. Compare Hunsrik transformeere.

noun:Teufelskreis.tx: From Teufel (“devil”) + Kreis (“circle”), a loose calque of Latin circulus vitiosus (also circulus diaboli, but possibly restricted to New Latin and then perhaps after the German).

noun:Totschlag.tx: From tot (“dead”) + Schlag (“blow, hit”). Compare Dutch doodslag.

noun:Trine.tx: From an abbreviation of the personal name Katharina.

noun:Torwart.tx: Formally from Middle High German torwart, torwarte (“doorkeeper, gatekeeper”), from Old High German torwart, torwarto (“doorkeeper, porter”). By surface analysis, Tor (“goal”) + Wart (“guardian”).

verb:teilnehmen.tx: From Teil (“part”) + nehmen (“take”). Calque of Latin participō, whence also English participate; compare corresponding calques such as Dutch deelnemen, English take part, Icelandic taka þátt. In this expression, the noun Teil (“part”) is considered verblasst (“grammaticalized”) and thus written lowercase when separated (Ich nehme teil).

verb:taxieren.tx: From north-western Middle High German taxieren (14th c.), from Middle Dutch taxeren (13th c.), from Latin taxāre.

verb:tippen.tx: From Middle Low German tippen (“to touch lightly”), from Middle Low German tip (“tip, fingertip”), cognate with English tip, from Proto-Germanic *tuppijô, *tuppijǭ (“tip”), diminutive of *tuppaz (“top”). Merged with Central and Low German tippen, dippen, düppen (“to dip, to dab, to tap”), from Proto-Germanic *dupjaną, cognate with tupfen and English dip. The sense “to type” is influenced by English type.

noun:Tropen.tx: A 19th-century borrowing from Ancient Greek τροπαί (tropaí), plural of τροπή (tropḗ, “turning; solstice”). Semantically after the earlier adjective tropisch, from Latin tropicus, from Ancient Greek τροπικός (tropikós).

noun:Tatu.tx: Ultimately from Old Tupi tatu; see English tatou. Displaced by Armadill and then by Gürteltier, which see.

noun:Topologie.tx: Coined by German mathematician Johann Benedict Listing in 1847, from Ancient Greek τόπος (tópos, “place, locality”) + -(o)logie (“study of, a branch of knowledge”).

noun:Torkel.tx: Old High German torcula, from Medieval Latin torcula, from torculum (“wine or olive press”).

intj:tschüss.tx: Borrowed from German Low German tschüß from earlier adjüs, from Dutch adjuus, from Spanish adiós or French adieu. (Compare the origin of moin.)

noun:Trapez.tx: Borrowed from Latin trapezium, from Ancient Greek τρᾰπέζῐον (trăpézĭon, “irregular quadrilateral”, literally “small table”), diminutive of τρᾰ́πεζα (trắpeza, “table”).

intj:topp.tx: Borrowed from Low German topp, perhaps related to Middle Low German toppen (“to beat”).

verb:tränken.tx: From Middle High German and Old High German trenken, from Proto-West Germanic *drankijan (“to cause to drink”). Cognate with Dutch drenken, English drench.

adj:tierisch.tx: From Middle High German [Term?], from Old High German [Term?]. By surface analysis, Tier (“animal”) + -isch (“-ic, -ish”).

noun:Traktat.tx: From Late Middle High German tractāt (14th c.), from Latin tractātus.

noun:Trinkgeld.tx: From Middle High German trincgelt. Equivalent to trinken (“to drink”) + Geld (“money”), meaning an extra to buy drinks with.

verb:trachten.tx: From Middle High German trahten, from Old High German trahtōn, from Proto-West Germanic *trahtōn, from Latin tractāre (“to drag, manage, handle”). Doublet of traktieren.

noun:Tourist.tx: Tour + -ist, towards the second half of the 18th century, possibly influenced by English tourist being formed around the same time.

noun:Tautologie.tx: Borrowed from Late Latin tautologia, from Ancient Greek ταὐτολογία (tautología); compare English tautology.

noun:Traktor.tx: With a relatinised pronunciation from English tractor, derived from Latin trahere (“to pull”).

adj:trächtig.tx: From Middle High German trehtic, trehtec, related to Middle Low German drechtich, drachtich. Equivalent to Tracht (“something carried”) + -ig. Cognate with Dutch drachtig, German Low German drachtig, Danish drægtig, Norwegian Bokmål drektig, Norwegian Nynorsk drektig, Swedish dräktig.

noun:Tachometer.tx: From Ancient Greek τᾰ́χος (tắkhos, “speed”) + μέτρον (métron, “something used to measure”), since the first half of the 19th century.

adv:trotzdem.tx: Univerbation of trotz + dem. Compare Middle High German tratz, traz, truz (“anyhow, nevertheless”).

conj:trotzdem.tx: Univerbation of trotz + dem. Compare Middle High German tratz, traz, truz (“anyhow, nevertheless”).

noun:Teelöffel.tx: From Tee (“tea”) + Löffel (“spoon”); cognate with Hunsrik Teeleffel.

noun:Tendenz.tx: Relatinized from French tendance under the influence of Medieval Latin tendentia.

adj:tendenziös.tx: Before 1850, from Tendenz + -iös. Compare English tendentious, French tendancieux (ca. 1900), both after the German.

noun:Trecker.tx: Phono-semantic matching of English tractor, whence also latinised German Traktor. After the Low German and Ripuarian verb trecken (“to drag, to pull”). Compare the same in Dutch trekker (“tractor”).

noun:Tribüne.tx: Borrowed from French tribune, from Italian tribuna.

noun:Theologie.tx: Borrowed from Latin theologia, from Ancient Greek θεολογία (theología). By surface analysis, theo- + -logie.

noun:Tatsache.tx: From Tat + Sache, calque of English matter of fact.

intj:Tatsache.tx: From Tat + Sache, calque of English matter of fact.

noun:Tentakel.tx: Borrowed from Latin tentāculum (“thing for feeling”).

noun:Tablett.tx: Borrowed from French tablette. Doublet of Tablet

adj:temporär.tx: Borrowed from French temporaire, from Latin temporārius, from tempus (“time”).

adv:temporär.tx: Borrowed from French temporaire, from Latin temporārius, from tempus (“time”).

noun:Tabelle.tx: From Late Latin tabella (“small table”), 16th c.

noun:Tagesordnung.tx: 18th century, from Tag (“day”) + -es- + Ordnung (“order”), a calque of French ordre du jour, itself apparently a calque of English order of the day.

noun:Tankstelle.tx: From tanken (“tank up, (re)fuel”) + Stelle (“place”), or Tank (“tank”) + Stelle (“place”).

adj:tragbar.tx: Derived from the verb tragen: trag- (“carry”) + -bar (“-able”)

verb:tüfteln.tx: Entered modern German from the Upper German language area. The exact origin is unclear. Grimm suggests a Rotwelsch origin (compare dufte). Kluge views it as a continuation of Middle High German tüfteln (“to knock, tap”).

noun:Trottel.tx: Of Austrian origin. The exact etymology is unknown but presumed to derive from trotteln (saunter, ramble, walk without a specific destination).

noun:Thema.tx: From Middle High German thema (14th c.), from Latin thema, from Ancient Greek θέμα (théma).

noun:Triangel.tx: From Latin triangulum. Compare Middle High German drīangel (“triangle”).

noun:Tagelöhner.tx: 15th century, from Tagelohn + -er, further analysable as Tag (“day”) + Lohn (“wage”) + -er.

verb:trainieren.tx: From English train + -ieren. Attested since the first half of the 19th century.

verb:trampen.tx: From English tramp, from Middle English trampen (“to walk heavily”), from Middle Low German trampen (“to stamp”) (trampeln (“to walk with heavy steps”), see English trample) or from Middle Dutch trampen (“to stamp”), from Proto-West Germanic *trampan (“to step”).

noun:Tramper.tx: Pseudo-anglicism, derived from English tramper or trampen + -er.

verb:tanken.tx: Borrowed from English tank. The reflexive use is from the now archaic sense "tank, armoured vehicle".

noun:Titte.tx: From Low German Titte (“nipple; breast”), from Middle Low German, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *titt- (“teat; nipple; breast”); according to Pokorny, this is ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *tata- (“father; parent; nipple”), though this is uncertain. In any case, all are of expressive origin. Doublet of Zitze, which was inherited. Cognate with Dutch tiet, English tit, teat. Borrowed into …

noun:Teuerung.tx: Inherited from Middle High German tiurunge (“price”), analyzable as teuer + -ung, though originally probably from a verb derivate that has not survived into New High German.

noun:Turnier.tx: From Late Middle High German turnier, alteration (after the verb turnieren) of older turnei, tornei, from Old French tornoi, itself deverbal from Old French tornoiier, tornier (“to turn, romp, fight in a tournament”), from torner (“to turn”), from Latin tornare (“to turn”).

noun:Tiegel.tx: From Middle High German tigel, tëgel, from Old High German tëgel, tëgal (“earthen vessel”), from Proto-Germanic *digulaz, of uncertain origin. Cognate with Dutch degel (“kettle, boiler, urn”), Danish digel (“crucible”), Swedish degel (“crucible”), Icelandic deigla (“melting pot; crucible”).

noun:Tischler.tx: From Middle High German tischler, tischlære.

verb:transferieren.tx: From Middle High German transferieren (14th c.), from Latin transferre. Influenced by English transfer.

noun:Terpentin.tx: From Middle Dutch terpentijn, from Old French terbentine, turbentine, Latin terebinthīna, from terebintha, from Ancient Greek τερεβινθίνη (terebinthínē), from τερεβινθινος (terebinthinos), from τερέβινθος (terébinthos). See also turpentine.

adj:töricht.tx: From Middle High German tœreht (also tōr-, -oht). By surface analysis, Tor (“fool”) + -icht.

verb:trocknen.tx: Deadjectival verb from trocken (“dry (adj.)”), i.e. trocken + -en

noun:Tagebau.tx: From Tag (“day”) + -e- + Bau (“building, winning, mining”). The first component refers to the (sun-lit) surface of the earth, as in the mining terms unter Tage (“below ground”) and über Tage (“above ground”). The second component is used in the sense of Abbau; compare Raubbau.

noun:Türkis.tx: From Middle High German turkoys, from Middle French turquoise.

verb:trommeln.tx: From late Middle High German trumelen, from a common Germanic word giving Danish tromme, Swedish trumma, English drum, etc., and ultimately of imitative origin.

noun:Trampeltier.tx: Deformation of Latin dromedarius, reanalysed by folk etymology as trampeln (“to trample”) + Tier (“a beast”). Doublet of Dromedar.

verb:trauern.tx: From Middle High German trūren, from Old High German trūrēn, from Proto-West Germanic *drūrēn. See Trauer (“mourning”).

noun:Tretmühle.tx: From Middle High German tretemüle, equivalent to treten + Mühle. In the sense of "fitness device", a calque of English treadmill.

noun:Turnhose.tx: From turnen 'to do gym' + Hose 'trousers, shorts'.

noun:Tinnitus.tx: Borrowed from Latin tinnītus. The first-syllable stress is from a generalisation of the tendency that penultimate Latin -i- is short; compare the same in Libido.

verb:tadeln.tx: From Middle High German tadelen. Equivalent to Tadel (“reproach”) + -en.

verb:tränen.tx: From Middle High German trahenen, trēnen, ultimately from the root of Träne (“tear”).

noun:Tragödie.tx: From Latin tragoedia, from Ancient Greek τραγῳδία (tragōidía, “epic play, tragedy”), from τράγος (trágos, “male goat”) + ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”), a reference to the goat-satyrs of the theatrical plays of the Dorians.

noun:Tölpel.tx: From a merger of dialectal tolp (with variants; of unknown, probably onomatopoetic, origin) and Middle High German dörpel, itself dissimilated from dörper, from Middle Low German dorper (“villager”), from dorp (“village”). Both of these words meant “rude, gruff person”, and dörper/dörpel particularly “uncultured, unrefined person”. The name of the bird is due to its apparently clumsy movements.

adj:tektonisch.tx: From Latin tectonicus, from Ancient Greek τεκτονικός (tektonikós). By surface analysis, Tektonik + -isch.

adj:treu.tx: From Middle High German triuwe, from Old High German triuwi, from Proto-West Germanic *triuwī, from Proto-Germanic *triwwiz. See English true for more.

noun:Trauring.tx: From trauen (“to wed”) + Ring (“ring”). Compare Dutch trouwring.

adj:traut.tx: From Middle High German trūt, from Old High German trūt, from Proto-West Germanic *drūd, from Proto-Germanic *drūdaz (“dear, beloved”). Compare Italian drudo, Dutch troetelen.

intj:tamam.tx: Borrowed from Turkish tamam, from Arabic تَمَام (tamām).

noun:Treffer.tx: From Middle High German treffer, treffære, equivalent to treffen (“to hit”) + -er.

noun:Taiga.tx: Borrowed from Russian тайга́ (tajgá), from Turkic or Yakut тайга (tayga).

noun:Tschusch.tx: Uncertain. Proposals are: From Serbo-Croatian čuješ (“you hear”); from Serbo-Croatian ćuš (“giddyup”); from Slovene čúš, from Turkish çavuş, which would make it a doublet of Tschausch.

noun:Takt.tx: Borrowed from Latin tāctus (“touch”). Sense “tact” via Semantic loan from French tact.

noun:Trank.tx: From Middle High German tranc, from Old High German tranc, from Proto-Germanic *drankiz (“drink; dose; potion”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰrenǵ- (“to pull; draw; sip”); compare Dutch drank (“beverage, drink”), Hunsrik Drank. In its general sense of "something to drink", it was displaced by Getränk.

noun:Tränke.tx: From Middle High German trenke, from Old High German trenka, from the root of tränken (“to water, make drink”), from Proto-Germanic *drankijaną.

noun:Truppe.tx: From French troupe, from Frankish *þorp, from Proto-Germanic *þurpą. Cognate with German Dorf (“village”).

noun:Todestrieb.tx: Coined by Sigmund Freud, Tod + -es- + Trieb

noun:Tarif.tx: From Arabic تَعَارِيف (taʕārīf, “fees to be paid”).

noun:Training.tx: Early 19th century, from English training. The pronunciation is influenced by related French traîner, entraîner.

noun:Thermosphäre.tx: From Ancient Greek θερμός (thermós, “warm, hot”) + Ancient Greek σφαῖρα (sphaîra, “ball, sphere”).

noun:Troposphäre.tx: From Ancient Greek τρόπος (trópos, “way, manner”) + Ancient Greek σφαῖρα (sphaîra, “ball, sphere”).

verb:trotten.tx: From Middle High German trotten (late 14th c.), from Old French trotter, troter (“to trot”). The French verb is possibly from Old High German trotōn (“to press wine”) or from a hypothetical Frankish *trottōn (“to tread”), both related with German treten. An alternative theory derives it from Latin tolutim (“trottingly”). See French trotter and English trot for more.

noun:Thorax.tx: From Ancient Greek θώραξ (thṓrax, “a breastplate, cuirass, corslet”).

verb:tagen.tx: From Middle High German tagen, from Old High German tagēn, from Proto-West Germanic *dagēn.

noun:Täter.tx: 15th century, backformation from the older pairs Missetäter/Übeltäter and Wohltäter/Guttäter. Equivalent to Tat (“deed”) + -er (“-er”, agent suffix). Compare Dutch dader (also a backformation).

noun:Tierschützer.tx: From Tier + Schützer (The latter term is a short form of Beschützer).

verb:trossen.tx: Related to Old French trosser (modern French trousser (“to tie up, to truss”)).

noun:Treibhausgas.tx: From Treibhaus (“greenhouse”) + Gas (“gas”), perhaps after English greenhouse gas.

verb:trollen.tx: Middle High German trollen, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *truzlōną (“to lumber”). Perhaps related to trödeln. Cognate of English troll.

verb:tuten.tx: From Low German and Middle Low German tūten, of imitative origin (lautmalend).

noun:Toxin.tx: From earlier Toxikum, a borrowing of Latin toxicum.

noun:Torlinie.tx: Tor (“goal”) + Linie (“line”), calque of English goal line.

verb:ticken.tx: In the meaning “to make a clicking noise” onomatopoeic. In the meaning “to sling” likely back-formed from verticken; mostly used by foreigners.

noun:Tjost.tx: Inherited by the late 12th century (Hartmann von Aue) from Middle High German tjost f, tjoste f, jiust f, jiuste f, joste f, schust f, but also (more rarely) as tust m, just m, just m, gust m, tschuscht m. From Old French jouster. Cognate with English joust.

adj:träge.tx: From Middle High German træge, from Old High German trāgi, from Proto-West Germanic *trāgī, from Proto-Germanic *trēgiz. Cognate to Dutch traag (“slow”).

noun:Trinität.tx: From Middle High German trinitāt, from Ecclesiastical Latin trinitās (genitive singular trinitātis).

noun:Tesafilm.tx: From Tesa + Film. The former is a trademark; see the lemma.

adv:teils.tx: From Teil (“part”) + -s (genitive suffix), originally an adverbial genitive.

noun:Totem.tx: Borrowed from English totem, from Ojibwe (o)doodem(an).

verb:trüben.tx: From Middle High German trüeben, from Old High German truoben, from Proto-West Germanic *drōbijan, from Proto-Germanic *drōbijaną.

adj:toxisch.tx: From obsolete Toxikum, a borrowing of Latin toxicum, with the adjectival suffix -isch.

noun:Thüringer.tx: Sidonius Apollinaris in 480 already has Toringus m (“(the/a) Thuringian”).

noun:Topas.tx: From Middle High German topāʒje, topāʒe, topaʒīus m or n, from Late Latin topāzius f, topāzion n, topāzōn m, from Classical topāzus f, topāzos f, from Ancient Greek τοπάζιον n (topázion), τόπαζος m (tópazos), probably named after Τόπαζος (Tópazos), ancient name of St. John's Island, Egypt, in the Red Sea, believed to be the first discovered source of the mineral peridot.

noun:Thermit.tx: Originally a brand name, from Ancient Greek θερμός (thermós, “heat”) + -it.

verb:tröpfeln.tx: From late Middle High German, from the predecessor of tropfen. Synchronically tropfen (“to drop, drip”) + -eln.

noun:Tran.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German trān (“tear”), from Old Saxon *trahn, Proto-West Germanic *trahnu (“tear”). Doublet of Träne.

adj:teigig.tx: Teig + -ig; similar to English doughy and Swedish degig.

noun:Theke.tx: Originally “cupboard, safe for the cash box”. From Low Franconian and West Central German dialects (attested early 16th century), probably through Middle Dutch teke (compare dated modern Dutch teek), from Latin thēca, from Ancient Greek θήκη (thḗkē). The word was introduced into modern standard German in the 19th century and remains more common in western Germany than elsewhere.

noun:Tattoo.tx: Borrowed from English tattoo. The rather common pronunciation with initial stress perhaps partly from a mistakenly assumed English form, but at least reinforced by the related words tätowieren, Tätowierung (both with unstressed -o- and often secondary stress on -ä-).

adj:tüchtig.tx: From Middle High German tühtec, from Old High German *tuhtig, from Proto-West Germanic *duhtīg. Cognate with Dutch duchtig (“considerable, large, sturdy, powerful”), English doughty, Danish dygtig (“virtuous, proficient”).

noun:Trauerspiel.tx: From Trauer + Spiel. Attested 1630, hence possibly after Dutch treurspel (1584).

noun:Tünnes.tx: West Central German form of the name Anton or Antonius. Compare the traditional Colognian humorous characters Tünnes un Schäl, where, however, Tünnes is a quirky, but not a ridiculous or stupid person.

noun:Tann.tx: From Middle High German tan(n) (“forest”), probably from the root of Tanne (“fir”).

noun:Tubus.tx: From Latin tubus. Doublet of Tube.

noun:Tatütata.tx: Onomatopoeia imitating the German police and ambulance siren (example here).

noun:Tohuwabohu.tx: Borrowed from Biblical Hebrew תוהו ובוהו (tōhū wā-ḇōhū) in Genesis 1:2, from תֹהוּ (tōhū, “formlessness, nothingness”) + בֹּהוּ (bōhū, “voidness, desolation”).

noun:Tücke.tx: From Middle High German tücke f, also tuc m (“conduct, procedure, move, trick”). Further origin unknown, perhaps expressive.

noun:Tacken.tx: Borrowed from German Low German Tack, Tacken (“jag, tooth”). Cognate with German Zacken (“idem”) and Dutch tak (“branch”). The modern sense is from mechanics, that is from machines in which different steps or stages are set by means of a gear wheel. Compare the German einen Zahn zulegen (“to hurry up”). Doublet of Zacke and Zacken.

noun:Trinkhalle.tx: Compound of trinken + Halle. It has been common practice in the region to consume drinks at kiosks (usually beer).

noun:Todestag.tx: From Tod + -es- + Tag. Compare Swedish dödsdag and English deathday, which are formed similarly.

noun:Täufer.tx: From Middle High German töufer, toufer, toufære, from Old High German toufāri. Analyzable as taufen + -er.

noun:Trappe.tx: From Middle High German trappe, possibly a borrowing from Slavic, from Proto-Slavic *dropъty, whose first part is probably from Proto-Indo-European *dreh₂- (“run”) and the other from Proto-Slavic *pъta (“bird”), which is probably based on Proto-Indo-European *put- (“a young, a child, a little animal”). See also Russian дрофа (drofa), Czech drop, Polish drop, Romanian dropie.

noun:Topp.tx: Ca. 1700, borrowed from German Low German Topp, from Middle Low German top, from Old Saxon *top, from Proto-West Germanic *topp. Doublet of Zopf (“bundle of hair”) and Top (“women’s shirt”).

noun:Trabant.tx: First attested in 1424. From Middle High German drabant (“Hussite foot soldier”), of unclear origin.

verb:tilgen.tx: From Middle High German tīlgen, tiligen, tīligen, from Old High German tiligōn, tīligōn, from Proto-West Germanic *diligōn. Compare also Old High German byforms dīlōn, tīlōn.

adj:trashig.tx: From Trash + -ig. Partial calque of English trashy.

noun:Traktorist.tx: Borrowed from Russian трактори́ст (traktoríst). By surface analysis, Traktor + -ist.

noun:Tempomat.tx: Blend of Tempo + Automat. Originally coined and trademarked by Mercedes-Benz, but has mostly entered common usage.

noun:Tattergreis.tx: tattern (“to shake, to tremble”) + Greis (“old man”)

noun:Tobel.tx: Middle High German tobel, from Old High German tobal (“valley, forest ravine”), from Proto-West Germanic *deup (“deep”).

noun:Tusch.tx: From tuschen (“to stike loudly, to clash”), with influence from French touche (“touch”).

noun:Trab.tx: From Middle High German drap, ultimately from the root of the verb traben (“to trot”).

noun:Top.tx: Borrowed from English top, of the same origin as inherited Zopf (“bundle of hair”) and, via Low German, Topp (“top of the mast”).

noun:Tandem.tx: Borrowed from English tandem, from Latin tandem (“at last”).

noun:Trübsal.tx: From Middle High German trüebesal, from Old High German truobisal (11th c.). Equivalent to trüb (“turbid, troubled, sad”) + -sal.

verb:tönen.tx: From Middle High German dœnen, *tœnen, derived from tōn, whence modern Ton (“tone, sound”).

noun:Tand.tx: From Middle High German tant (“idle talk, tricks”), of unclear origin, possibly a Romance borrowing, compare Spanish tanto (“purchase price”, literally “so much”). Cognate with Bavarian Tand, Danish tant, Norwegian Bokmål tant.

verb:tupfen.tx: From Middle High German tüpfen, tupfen (“to dip, to moisten”), from Old High German tuphen (“to dip, to moisten”), from Proto-Germanic *dupjaną; see *daupijaną (“to dip”). Cognate with English dip. The semantic development is due to association with Middle High German stuphen (“to poke”) and a dialectal (Central German) merger with unrelated tippen (“to tap”).

noun:Tagesschau.tx: From Tag (“day”) + -es- + Schau (“show”), formed after Wochenschau (“weekly cinema newsreel”).

verb:taumeln.tx: From Middle High German tūmeln, from Old High German tūmalōn, tūmilōn, frequentative of tūmōn, either from Proto-Indo-European *dʰewh₂- (“to fume”) or related to Dunst (“haze”). Related with Dutch tuimelen, English tumble, but the phonetics of this root are unclear, as is its relation with Romance words such as French tomber, Spanish tumbar and Portuguese tombar.

noun:Taumel.tx: From Middle High German tū̆meln (“to reel, stagger”), Old High German tūmalōn (“to turn”).

noun:Than.tx: Borrowed from English thane. Related to archaic German Degen (“hero”).

noun:Trotte.tx: From treten (“to tread”), probably modeled after Latin calcātūra, compare Kelter.

noun:Truthuhn.tx: From trut + Huhn (“chicken”), after older Truthahn; see there.

noun:Treibgut.tx: treiben (“to drift, to float”) + Gut (“goods, commodity”)

noun:Tupfen.tx: Originally the plural of Tupf, from Middle High German topfe, from Old High German topho, ultimately related to the root of tupfen (“to dab”).

adj:tagtäglich.tx: Tag + täglich, with the reduplication serving for emphasis.

noun:Tenne.tx: From Middle High German tenne, from Old High German tenni, from Proto-West Germanic *dani (“flat area; pasture”). Cognate with English den.

adj:tobsüchtig.tx: From Middle High German tobesühtic. Equivalent to Tobsucht + -ig.

adj:transzendent.tx: Borrowed from Latin trānscendēns, present participle of trānscendō.

adj:triftig.tx: Inherited from Middle High German triftic.

adj:trunken.tx: Inherited from Middle High German trunken, from Old High German trunkan. Originally an unprefixed past participle of trinken. Largely displaced by betrunken in the 18th century.

adj:töfte.tx: Related to dufte, from Hebrew טוֹב (tov, “good”);

noun:Trester.tx: From Middle High German trëster, from Old High German trestir, originally a plural of a *trast, from Proto-West Germanic *drast. Cognate with English drest.

noun:Tacheles.tx: Borrowed from Yiddish תּכלית (takhles, “purpose, result”), from Hebrew תכלית (takhlít, “end, purpose”).

noun:Trift.tx: From Middle High German trift (“driving, floating, way of living”), from Old High German *trift, from Proto-Germanic *driftiz, deverbal from *drībaną (“to drive”), whence German treiben. Doublet of Drift (from Low German), whose nautical senses were also added to Trift as semantic loans (now uncommon).

noun:Traufe.tx: A shortened form of the term Dachtraufe, Middle High German trouf(e), Old High German trouf.

noun:Taugenichts.tx: From taugen (“to be of use”) + nichts (“nothing”), alteration of older tügenicht (1548), itself perhaps after Middle Low German dögenicht (1514); compare Dutch deugniet (1539). The two earliest High German attestations are apparently in authors from the Low German borderland: 1548 in Burkard Waldis from Allendorf (who also lived in Low German Riga), and 1563 in Joachim Westphal from the area of …

verb:trudeln.tx: Probably a derivative of trendeln (“to roll”), itself a verbal from Trendel (“curve; spinning top”) (DWDS); see the related English trendel for more.

noun:Trosse.tx: From Middle Low German trosse and ultimately related to Dutch tros.

noun:Tresen.tx: From Middle High German trëse, from Old High German trëso (“treasure, treasury”), from Old French tresor, which see. Originally referred to a cash box, then shifting to the desk on which such a box would be situated. Doublet of Tresor and Thesaurus.

noun:Trivialität.tx: Borrowed from French trivialité. Compare English triviality.

verb:triezen.tx: From Low German tritzen (and variants). Equivalent to Trieze (“winch”) + -en. The modern sense is figurative from the nautical punishment.

noun:Teckel.tx: 18th c., from Low German Teckel, a variant of German Dackel, also Dächsel and perhaps *Däckel, from Dachshund. Most readily explained as a borrowing from Upper German or East Central German dialects, which use the diminutive ending -el and in which word-initial ‹d› tends to be voiceless. Note, however, that Teckel is attested somewhat earlier than the other forms.

verb:tummeln.tx: From Middle High German tumeln, from a different ablaut form of the root that also gives taumeln (“to sway, teeter”). Cognate with Bavarian tummln and Luxembourgish tommelen.

noun:Truthenne.tx: From trut + Henne (“hen, female chicken”), after older Truthahn; see there.

verb:tünchen.tx: From Middle High German tünichen, from Old High German tunihhōn, derived from tunihha, from Latin tunica.

noun:Twen.tx: Clipping of English twenty, probably influenced by teen.

verb:totlachen.tx: From tot + lachen. Compare West Frisian dealaitsje, Dutch doodlachen.

verb:traktieren.tx: 15th century, from Latin tractare. Compare Dutch trakteren, French traiter, English treat. Doublet of trachten.

verb:trippeln.tx: From now-obsolete trippen + -eln. Ultimately an ablaut variation of imitative verbs trappen, trappeln.

noun:Truchsess.tx: From Middle High German truhtsæze (“steward”), from Old High German truhtsāzzo, compound of trucht (“host”) + sazzo (“one who sits”). The first part goes back to Proto-Germanic *druhtiz (“troop”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰrewgʰ- (“to support”). Doublet of Drost (“reeve, bailiff”).

noun:Tollpatsch.tx: First attested 1698 in Bavaria as Tolbatz, from Hungarian talpas (“wide-footed; infantryman”), so called because of their footwear consisting of soles attached by strings. Influenced by toll (“crazy”), patschen (“to whoosh, to hit with a splashing sound”), and dalpen, talpen (“to walk clumsily; to grab clumsily”), also Dalpe, Talpe, Dalpsche, Talpsche, Patsche, designations for a broad hand.

noun:Tabernakel.tx: From Middle High German tabernakel, from Old French tabernacle, from Latin tabernāculum.

verb:tändeln.tx: From Middle High German tand (“idle chatter”); related to Tand (“trifles”). Compare English dandle.

noun:Tuchfühlung.tx: From Tuch (“cloth, fabric”) + Fühlung (“touching, contact”), literally “a contact close enough to touch someone’s clothes”. Originally used in military contexts, especially in precision marching, where it refers to the perfect distance between marchers, namely such that the edges of their sleeves touch but not their arms.

noun:Tagwerk.tx: From Middle High German tagewerc, tagewerch, from Old High German tagawerk, from Proto-Germanic *dagawerką. Cognate with English daywork. Equivalent to Tag + Werk. The measure of land corresponds to the area that can be ploughed in a day by a team of oxen.

noun:Trunkenbold.tx: From Middle High German trunkenbolt. Analyzable as trunken + -bold.

verb:tunken.tx: With irregular devoicing from Middle High German dunken, from Old High German thunkōn, whence also (through Pennsylvania German) English dunk.

noun:Tesa.tx: From the trademarked brand name Tesa, also tesa. Formed in 1906 by Elsa Tesmer, then an administrative officer at Beiersdorf, after the first and last syllables of her name (Tesmer, Elsa).

noun:Tornister.tx: 17th century, from slightly earlier Tanister, from Czech tanystra (now obsolete), from Hungarian tanisztra (and variants, now tarisznya). Further from Medieval Greek τάγιστρον (tágistron, “nosebag”), or Latin canistrum (“wicker basket”), or a merger of both. The change of the first syllable from Ta- to Tor- in German is probably from dialectal influence (either directly or by way of hypercorrection).

noun:Trauerarbeit.tx: Trauer (“mourning”) + Arbeit (“work”), coined by Sigmund Freud.

noun:Tretroller.tx: Compound of treten (“to tread”) + Roller (a derivation of rollen).

noun:Tobsucht.tx: From Middle High German tobesuht. By surface analysis, toben + Sucht.

noun:Tross.tx: Inherited from Middle High German trosse (“baggage”), from Old French trosse, trousse (“package, bundle”). The semantic development from “baggage” to “those who move the baggage” occurred around 1500. Cognate with English truss, which see.

noun:Therme.tx: 16th century, from Latin thermae, from Ancient Greek θερμά (thermá).

noun:Treck.tx: From Low German treck, from Middle Low German trek, from Old Saxon *trekan, from Proto-Germanic *trekaną, *trakjaną (“to drag, haul, scrape, pull”), from Proto-Indo-European *dreg- (“to drag, scrape”). Cognate with English trek.

noun:Trulla.tx: Perhaps a feminised form of dialectal Upper German Trull, Troll (“coarse, boorish person”), which is probably inherited from Proto-Germanic *truzlą. Cognate with Troll (“troll”), from Old Norse.

verb:torkeln.tx: From late Middle High German torkeln, from Late Latin torculo (“to press”), a derivation of Latin torculum (“wine press”).

noun:Talmi.tx: Pseudo-Gallicism created as a trade name in Austria or Bavaria.

noun:Teenie.tx: Possibly from Teen, influenced by English teeny (“tiny”) and -i

verb:tatschen.tx: From a variant of Middle High German tetschen, of imitative origin. Compare also patschen, klatschen. Not related with English touch (except to the degree that the underlying Latin *tuccāre may ultimately also be imitative).

noun:Turtel.tx: From Middle High German turtel, ultimately from Latin turtur.

verb:träufeln.tx: träufen + -eln, the former a causative form of triefen.

noun:Tonicwasser.tx: Partial calque of English tonic water.

noun:Töle.tx: 17th century, from Low German Töle. Further origin uncertain. Plausibly from an old, though unattested, diminutive of Middle Low German tō (“bitch, female dog”), in the form of an Old Saxon *tōhila. The Middle Low German is cognate with archaic German Zohe (“bitch”), perhaps related with ziehen (“to pull, rear”).

phrase:tief in die Tasche greifen.tx: Literally, “to dig deep in one's pocket”.

noun:Tändelei.tx: tändeln (“to dally, to flirt”) + -ei (denoting a condition)

noun:Typhus.tx: 19th century, from Latin typhus, from Ancient Greek τῦφος (tûphos).

noun:Tute.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German tûte (“conical object”). Doublet of Tüte. It is usually thought that the verb tuten (“to toot, hoot”) is an originally unrelated onomatopoeia, though both words have certainly influenced each other. Alternatively, the verb might have been derived from the noun or vice versa. Related to English tote.

noun:Tinnef.tx: Borrowed from Yiddish טנוף (tinef) (via Rotwelsch), from Hebrew טִנּוּף (tinnúf, “trash”).

noun:Trense.tx: 16th century, from Early Modern Dutch trense (now trens), from Spanish trenza.

noun:Tagesgericht.tx: From Tag (“day”) + -es- + Gericht (“dish”). Compare Dutch dagschotel.

noun:Talkmaster.tx: Talk(show) + English master, modelled after Showmaster.

noun:Toches.tx: Borrowed from Yiddish תּחת (tokhes, “buttocks”), in turn from Hebrew תַּחַת (tákhat, “buttocks”).

noun:Thinktank.tx: An unadapted borrowing from English thinktank.

noun:Tollheit.tx: From Middle High German tolheit, toleheit, from Old High German tolaheit, since the 9th century. By surface analysis, toll + -heit.

noun:Translator.tx: Borrowed from Latin translator, probably after English translator or French translateur (cp. Translateur).

noun:Taverne.tx: From Middle High German taverne, from Italian taverna and/or Old French taverne.

noun:Tarte.tx: Fairly recent borrowing from French tarte.

noun:Token.tx: Borrowed from English token. Doublet of Zeichen.

noun:Talar.tx: From Latin tālāria or Italian talare.

noun:Tankwart.tx: Shortened from Tankstellenwart. Analysable as tanken (“to refuel”) + Wart (“guard, keeper”).

noun:Triple.tx: 20th century, from French triple (after Double). Semantically following English treble.

noun:Taxameter.tx: Coined in German from Medieval Latin taxa (“tax, charge”) and -meter.

verb:telegraphieren.tx: Borrowed from French télégraphier. Equivalent to Telegraph + -ieren.

noun:Texteditor.tx: From Text + Editor, a calque of English text editor.

noun:Trug.tx: From Middle High German trüge, from Old High German trugī. Cf. trügen.

pt: to split, to share, to divide
noun:Teiler.tx: From Middle High German teiler, from Old High German teilāri, from Proto-West Germanic [Term?]; compare Old English dælere, Middle Dutch dêelre. By surface analysis, teilen (“to split, to share, to divide”) + -er.

noun:Tunika.tx: Borrowed from Latin tunica. Doublet of Tünche.

adj:teilhaftig.tx: From Middle High German teilhaftic, teilheftic. Analyzable as Teil + -haftig. Compare teilhaben.

noun:Todesschwadron.tx: From Tod + -es- + Schwadron. Contemporary use probably after English death squad. Occasionally attested before the 20th century in the sense “suicide squad” (formation executing a highly risky command).

noun:Tanker.tx: From tanken + -er, possibly reinforced by English tanker.

noun:Töter.tx: From Middle High German tœter, equivalent to töten + -er

noun:Tacke.tx: From Middle High German tacke, from Old High German tacha, from Proto-Germanic *dakkōną, related to Proto-Germanic *dōkaz (“cloth, rag”). Compare Bavarian Tackn, Dackn.

noun:Trödel.tx: The compound Trödelmarkt is first attested in the 15th century as East Central German dredelmarckt, but further etymology is unknown.

noun:Todeslos.tx: From Tod (“death”) + -es- + Los (“lot”). The sports sense after Todesgruppe.

noun:Triptychon.tx: From Ancient Greek τρίπτυχον (tríptukhon), neuter singular of τρίπτυχος (tríptukhos).

noun:Terrier.tx: Ultimately from Middle French, from Old French chien terrier (“terrier dog”), from chien (“dog”) + Old French terrier (“of earth”, adjective), from Medieval Latin terrarius (“of earth”), from Latin terra (“earth”).

verb:trillern.tx: From Italian trillo, trillare. Compare Middle High German trillieren. Cognate with English trill.

noun:Trill.tx: Unadapted borrowing from English trill. Doublet of Triller.

phrase:the yellow from the egg.tx: Back-formation from my English is not the yellow from the egg, but it goes.

noun:Trieze.tx: Late 18th century, from Low German Trieze (also Tritze, Trisse, Trietsche), from Middle Low German tritze, trisse (vowel short and long). Cognate with Dutch trijs, English trice. Further origin unknown.

phrase:tausend Dank.tx: Literally, “a thousand thanks”. Compare Swedish tusen tack etc.

noun:Tapioka.tx: From Brazilian Portuguese tapioca, from Old Tupi tapi'oka.

noun:Trucker.tx: Borrowed from American English trucker. By surface analysis, Truck + -er.

noun:Turn.tx: Borrowed from English turn. Doublet of Törn.

verb:tuckern.tx: 20th century, from Low German tuckern (“to throb, pulsate”, 19th c.), iterative of tucken (“to jerk, twitch, beat, hit”), which is cognate with Dutch tokken, tukken, German zucken, zücken, and thus ultimately related to ziehen (“to pull”). The semantic development within Low German as well as the adoption into Standard German were reinforced by the word’s onomatopoeic quality.

noun:Tappert.tx: From Middle High German taphart, daphart, tappart, from Medieval Latin tabardum, from Old French tabard.

noun:Tonie.tx: Ton + diminutive suffix -i, with alternate spelling "-ie". Genericized trademark of the proprietary name owned by Tonies SE.

noun:Teleportation.tx: From English teleportation. By surface analysis, teleportieren + -ation.

phrase:täglich grüßt das Murmeltier.tx: Literally, “the marmot greets daily”. From the German title of the 1993 US film Groundhog Day.

noun:Technokrat.tx: Borrowed from English technocrat, equivalent to techno- + -krat.

noun:Tauwerk.tx: From Tau (“strong rope”) + Werk (“work, accessories”), likely calqued on either Dutch touwwerk (ca. 1600) or Low German. Compare Danish tovværk, Norwegian tauverk.

noun:Täubling.tx: Perhaps related to Taube (“dove”), from its color.

noun:Taschner.tx: From Middle High German taschener. By surface analysis, Tasche (“bag”) + -ner.
